You'd get the most for the least work from **one long-lived pod running a multi-session daemon**, not a pod per agent.

**Recommended: Paseo daemon in a StatefulSet**
- It already has what you listed: a CLI, a mobile app, and many concurrent agents that you create and destroy from either surface.
- Agents are processes inside the daemon, so spinning one up or down never touches Kubernetes. The cluster only sees one pod.
- Run it as a single-replica StatefulSet. Give it a PVC for repos and worktrees, and mount `~/.claude` credentials from a SOPS secret.
- Expose it on `envoy-internal`. For mobile access away from home, use a Tailscale sidecar or `envoy-external` behind Cloudflare Access, not a bare public route.
- It fits your existing `kubernetes/apps/<ns>/<app>` layout, so it's a normal `flux-deploy` job.
- The catch is that all agents share one pod's CPU and memory. Set generous limits and keep each repo in its own worktree.

**Pod per agent**
- This isolates agents, but you'd need a controller or CRD, such as kubernetes-sigs/agent-sandbox, plus your own chat front end.

  ## Claude Code Remote Control: research report
  
  Sources were read directly from code.claude.com. The Remote Control page is https://code.claude.com/docs/en/remote-control.md, the CLI reference is https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference.md, and the auth page is https://code.claude.com/docs/en/authentication.md. The docs map at https://code.claude.com/docs/en/claude_code_docs_map.md has no separate server-mode or Docker/Kubernetes page, and I found no official container or Kubernetes guidance for Remote Control.
  
  ### 1. CLI flags and subcommands (confirmed in docs)
  
  Three invocation modes exist:
  - `claude remote-control`: server mode. It runs with no local interactive session and waits for remote connections.
  - `claude --remote-control` / `--rc [name]`: an interactive session with Remote Control on.
  - `/remote-control` / `/rc [name]`: slash command from an existing session, also available in the VS Code extension and the Desktop app.
  
  Server-mode flags, all from the remote-control.md "Server mode" tab:
  - `--name "My Project"`: session title.
  - `--remote-control-session-name-prefix <prefix>`: prefix for auto names. Default is the hostname. Env var `CLAUDE_REMOTE_CONTROL_SESSION_NAME_PREFIX` does the same.
  - `-c`, `--continue`: bring back the session this server started with (requires v2.1.200+).
  - `--session-id <id>`: bring back one session by ID (requires v2.1.200+).
  - `--spawn <mode>`:
    - `same-dir` (default when no mode is saved): all sessions share the cwd and can conflict.
    - `worktree`: each on-demand session gets its own git worktree. Requires a git repo or a `WorktreeCreate` hook.
    - `session`: serves exactly one session and rejects extra connections. Startup only.
    - Press `w` at runtime to toggle same-dir and worktree.
  - `--capacity <N>`: maximum concurrent sessions. Default 32. Cannot be used with `--spawn=session`.
  - `--[no-]create-session-in-dir`: pre-creates one session in the cwd at startup. On by default.
  - `--permission-mode <mode>`: starting permission mode for the server's sessions, for example `acceptEdits`. `manual` is an alias for `default`.
  - `--chrome` / `--no-chrome` (v2.1.273+).
  - `-d`, `--debug[=filter]` (v2.1.282+), `--debug-file <path>`, `--verbose`.
  - `--sandbox` / `--no-sandbox`: removed in v2.1.300. Passing either makes the server exit with an error. Enable sandboxing through a settings file instead.
  
  Other behaviour:
  - Global `claude` flags placed before `remote-control` are not carried into the spawned sessions. Some, such as `--verbose` and `--model`, pass through. Others, such as `--settings`, make it refuse to start.
  - `claude remote-control --help` prints the flags.
  
  Related CLI commands from cli-reference.md:
  - `claude remote-control`: the server. Its table entry says "Runs in server mode (no local interactive session)."
  - `claude auth login [--email] [--sso] [--console]`: `--console` signs in for API billing, which Remote Control does not support.
  - `claude auth status [--text]`: exits 0 if logged in. Its JSON `authMethod` can be `none`, `claude.ai`, `oauth_token`, `api_key`, `api_key_helper`, or `third_party`.
  - `claude setup-token`: generates a one-year OAuth token. Explained below.
  - `claude doctor`: includes Remote Control eligibility checks.
  - `claude mcp login <name> --no-browser`: prints a connector auth URL over SSH.
  - `claude daemon run|status|logs` and `claude agents` relate to background sessions, not Remote Control.
  
  Server-mode settings and environment variables:
  - Settings: `remoteControlAtStartup` (true/false, read from user or managed settings; project settings can only set false), `disableRemoteControl`, and `dialogExpiry`.
  - Env vars: `CLAUDE_CLIENT_PRESENCE_FILE` (suppresses phone pushes while the file exists) and `CLAUDE_REMOTE_CONTROL_SESSION_NAME_PREFIX`.
  
  ### 2. Creating and ending sessions: phone or web vs terminal (confirmed)
  
  - Server mode prints a URL and a QR code. Press spacebar to toggle the QR code. The session list at claude.ai/code or in the Claude mobile app (tap Code) shows sessions with a green dot.
  - New sessions started from claude.ai/code or the app are created on demand. In `worktree` mode each gets its own worktree. In `same-dir` mode they share the cwd.
  - Ending a session:
    - Stopping the server with Ctrl+C makes its sessions stop responding. They are not archived if no other `remote-control` is running in that directory and `--no-create-session-in-dir` was not used.
    - Sessions can be archived or deleted from another device or app. The docs say "the server no longer reports this session: it may have been deleted from another device or app." Archived sessions can be found at claude.ai/code.
  - Resuming after the server stops (within about 4 hours):
    - `claude remote-control` in the same directory brings back all served sessions.
    - `--continue` brings back one session.
    - `--session-id` brings back one session.
    - After about 4 hours, a new `claude remote-control` starts fresh sessions.
  - Crashed sessions in server mode are served again when a message is sent from a connected device (v2.1.238+). The server does not need a restart.
  - Interactive sessions can be disconnected with `/remote-control` again.
  - The docs say no specific cap applies to the total number of sessions across the whole server.
  
  ### 3. Auth for headless or container use (mostly confirmed, with a gap)
  
  Confirmed requirements:
  - Subscription: Pro, Max, Ultra, Team, or Enterprise. API keys are not supported.
  - On Team and Enterprise, an Owner must enable the Remote Control toggle in admin settings. ZDR and HIPAA organizations cannot enable it.
  - You must be logged in with `/login` (claude.ai). `claude remote-control` exits with an error without an eligible login.
  - Errors that name these credentials block Remote Control:
    - `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, or `apiKeyHelper` cause "Remote Control requires claude.ai subscription auth." Remove them from the shell environment and from settings `env`.
    - `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` from `claude setup-token` cannot establish Remote Control. The docs say these tokens "can only make model requests." This is confirmed from both the authentication and remote-control pages. The error is "Remote Control requires a full-scope login token."
  - Cloud providers such as Bedrock, Vertex, and Foundry are not supported. Neither is an `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` pointing somewhere other than `api.anthropic.com`, nor an enterprise Claude apps gateway sign-in.
  - Credential storage is documented: Linux keeps the login in `~/.claude/.credentials.json` with mode 0600. `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` moves that location. macOS uses the Keychain, with the file as a fallback.
  
  Gaps and uncertainties (not documented):
  - Whether a `.credentials.json` produced by `/login` on another machine can be mounted into a pod and used by Remote Control. The docs describe the file's location and permissions but do not say it is supported for this. Refresh-token rotation may also cause two copies to diverge. I could not confirm this either way.
  - Whether `claude auth login` has a headless or device-code mode. The CLI reference shows only `--email`, `--sso`, and `--console`. The only documented no-browser path is `--no-browser` on `claude mcp login`. I could not confirm a non-browser login for `claude auth login`.
  - The docs say a login that expires while an unattended session runs stops making progress until the user runs `/login` again. Expiry is shown as a warning three days ahead.
  
  ### 4. Limitations (confirmed)
  
  - One remote session per interactive process. Use server mode for multiple concurrent sessions from one process.
  - The local `claude` process must keep running. The session is offline if the process stops. Run `claude` inside `tmux` or `screen` over SSH.
  - Network: the process makes outbound HTTPS only (port 443 to the Anthropic API). It registers with the API and polls for work. No inbound ports are opened. The docs say "Remote Control requires access to the Anthropic API on port 443."
  - Server mode gives up after about 10 minutes of network outage and exits. Interactive sessions retry indefinitely.
  - Permission prompts: permission prompts and `AskUserQuestion` are forwarded to the remote client and wait until answered. Other forwarded dialogs expire after 5 minutes by default, controlled by `dialogExpiry`. The docs do not say how permission prompts behave when there is no remote client. ## Docker Paseo: Reference

**Image and ports**
- Image: `ghcr.io/getpaseo/paseo:latest`. The `latest` tag tracks the latest stable release, not a `main` build.
- Port: `6767`. The daemon listens on `0.0.0.0:6767` inside the container and serves the bundled web UI from the same origin.
- Web UI: `http://localhost:6767`

**Environment variables**
- `PASEO_PASSWORD`: Enables password auth for the daemon API and WebSocket. Set it for any published or network-reachable deployment.
- `PASEO_HOSTNAMES`: Allows DNS names to reach the daemon, for example `"paseo.example.com,.lan"`. IPs and `localhost` are allowed by default. Without it, DNS-name access returns `403 Host not allowed`.

**Volumes**

| Mount | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `/home/paseo` | Daemon state in `/home/paseo/.paseo`, plus agent config and credentials such as `.codex` and `.claude` |
| `/workspace` | Code that Paseo and launched agents can read and write |

On Linux, the `paseo` user is uid/gid `1000:1000`. Make mounted directories writable by that user, or use Docker's `--user` option (Compose: `user:`).

**Run**

```bash
docker run -d --name paseo \
  -p 6767:6767 \
  -e PASEO_PASSWORD=REDACTED \
  -v "$PWD/paseo-home:/home/paseo" \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace" \
  ghcr.io/getpaseo/paseo:latest
```

**Docker Compose**

```yaml
services:
  paseo:
    image: ghcr.io/getpaseo/paseo:latest
    container_name: paseo
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "6767:6767"
    environment:
      PASEO_PASSWORD: "REDACTED"
      # PASEO_HOSTNAMES: "paseo.example.com,.lan"
    volumes:
      - ./paseo-home:/home/paseo
      - ./workspace:/workspace
```

```bash
docker compose up -d
```

**Installing agent CLIs**

The base image does not include agent CLIs such as Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Copilot, Pi, or Muse Code. Build a child image:

```Dockerfile
FROM ghcr.io/getpaseo/paseo:latest

USER root
RUN npm install -g @openai/codex @anthropic-ai/claude-code opencode-ai
```

```bash
docker build -t paseo-with-agents .
```

Then set `image: paseo-with-agents` in Compose. Keep the child image's user as root. The entrypoint uses root only for first-run volume setup, then drops the daemon and agents to `paseo`.

**Claude Code authentication**

The page doesn't include a Claude-specific auth flow. It describes two general options:
- Pass provider environment variables. The page doesn't name the variables for Claude.
- Run the provider login inside the container:

## Relay

- **Config key:** `daemon.relay.enabled`
- **Default:** New homes write `daemon.relay.enabled: false`. If you remove the field from a new home, relay stays disabled. A daemon that started without the field keeps the legacy relay-enabled behavior, so set the field explicitly when editing an older config.
- **Disable it:**

```json
{
  "daemon": {
    "relay": {
      "enabled": false
    }
  }
}
```

Then run `paseo reload`. Relay enablement is runtime-safe, so no restart is needed.

- **Foreground override:** `PASEO_RELAY_ENABLED=false` overrides the file for a foreground deployment. Managed `start` reads the file only.
- **Endpoint:** This page doesn't name a config key for the relay endpoint. It only says relay endpoints and TLS require a restart. See [Connectivity](/docs/connectivity) and [Security](/docs/security).

## Password authentication for direct connections

When a password is set, all HTTP and WebSocket clients must authenticate. Only `/api/health` is exempt.

- **Set it:** Run `paseo daemon set-password`. This writes a bcrypt hash to `config.json`. Restart the daemon afterward.
- **Alternatives:** Set `PASEO_PASSWORD` (plaintext, hashed at startup), or write a hash to `daemon.auth.password`.
- **CLI connection:** Embed the password in the URI, or set the env var as a fallback:

```bash
paseo --host "tcp://192.168.1.10:6767?password=my-secret" ls
PASEO_PASSWORD=my-secret paseo ls
```

A `password=` in the URI takes precedence over the env var.

- **Mobile app:** Enter the password on the direct connection setup screen.

## daemon.listen and hostnames

- **Listen address:** `daemon.listen`, for example `"127.0.0.1:6767"`. Override with `PASEO_LISTEN`. Changes require a restart.
- **Allowed hostnames:** `daemon.hostnames`, for example `["localhost", ".localhost"]`. Override or extend with `PASEO_HOSTNAMES`. Changes apply on reload.
- **Deprecated alias:** `daemon.allowedHosts` and `PASEO_ALLOWED_HOSTS` still work but are deprecated.
- **Merging:** List settings append across sources, so values in `config.json` still apply when an env var is set.

## TLS/SSL

This page doesn't document any TLS configuration keys or certificate options. It only notes that relay endpoints and TLS are startup settings that require a restart, and that deployment overrides can control them.

**What the relay sees and where it runs**

The daemon connects outbound to the relay, and your phone meets it there. The docs name the official relay as the open-source Elixir service at [getpaseo/paseo-relay](https://github.com/getpaseo/paseo-relay), but they don't say where it's hosted. The relay can see metadata but not content. "The relay sees only: IP addresses, timing, message sizes, and session IDs." Message contents are end-to-end encrypted, so the relay can't read them.

**Ensuring the relay is disabled**

Relay is off on new installations. When you pair a device, Paseo asks before enabling it. To keep it off:

- Decline the prompt when pairing through `paseo`, `paseo daemon pair`, or Paseo Desktop.
- Don't pass `--relay` to the CLI pairing or startup commands, since that opts in without a prompt.

Declining also means no pairing QR code is created. The daemon remains available for direct TCP, Tailscale, or other VPN connections.

**Direct connection security**

- **Keep the default bind unless you need more.** By default, the daemon listens on `127.0.0.1:6767`, which is localhost only.
- **Consider a socket file for maximum isolation.** It blocks all network access, but the CLI is the only client that supports it.
- **Set a password before binding to a network.** Without one, any client that can reach the address can connect. Password auth controls access but does not encrypt traffic.
- **Avoid binding to `0.0.0.0`.** It exposes the daemon on every interface, including public Wi-Fi. If you must, use firewall rules and review your `hostnames` configuration.
- **Don't rely on CORS.** It doesn't prevent DNS rebinding. Paseo's host allowlist (`daemon.hostnames`) is the protection against that.

**VPN advice**

Use a VPN such as Tailscale for direct access outside your local network. "The VPN encrypts the traffic and keeps the daemon off the public internet." Then:

1. Bind the daemon to its VPN address.
2. Set a Paseo password.
3. Add that address as a direct connection in the client.

The page doesn't mention devcontainers, Docker, containers, or Nix. Environment consistency comes from `paseo.json` setup commands, copied files, and per-worktree service and port configuration.

**Setup and teardown (`paseo.json`)**
- `worktree.setup` runs once after the worktree is created, typically to install dependencies. Example: `"setup": "npm ci\nnpm run db:migrate"`.
- `worktree.teardown` runs during archive, before the directory is removed.
- Both accept a multiline shell script or an array of commands, run sequentially, with the worktree as the working directory.
- `paseo.json` is read from the committed version of the base branch you picked, so uncommitted changes on other branches don't apply.
- `.worktreeinclude` copies selected gitignored files, such as `.env`, from the source checkout before setup runs.
- Plugin hooks `worktree.create.before` and `worktree.create.after` can adjust placement or write files before setup.

**Scripts**
- `scripts` defines named commands, such as `"test": { "command": "npm test" }`, that you run on demand inside a worktree.

**Services**
- A script with `"type": "service"` is supervised as a long-running process and gets a port.
- `port` is optional. Omit it to have Paseo auto-assign one.
- Bind to `$PASEO_PORT` instead of hard-coding a port so each worktree's copy of a service gets a distinct port.
- Services are reachable through a daemon reverse proxy at deterministic hostnames like `http://<script>--<branch>--<project>.localhost:<daemon-port>`.
- Port ranges come from `worktrees.servicePorts.range` (global) or `worktree.servicePorts.range` (per project). `worktree.servicePorts.portScript` points to an external allocator executable. An explicit `port` overrides both.

**Environment variables**
- All of setup, teardown, scripts, and services get `$PASEO_SOURCE_CHECKOUT_PATH`, `$PASEO_WORKTREE_PATH`, and `$PASEO_BRANCH_NAME`.
- Services also get `$PASEO_PORT`, `$PASEO_URL`, `$PASEO_SERVICE_<NAME>_PORT` and `_URL` for peer services, and `$HOST`.
- `$PASEO_WORKTREE_PORT` is legacy; the page recommends `$PASEO_PORT` inside services.

**Terminals**
- `worktree.terminals` opens named terminals with commands when a worktree is created.

**Per-worktree consistency**
Each worktree gets its own directory and branch, and the same `paseo.json` setup runs in each. Services get distinct ports and proxy URLs, and peer services find each other through the `PASEO_SERVICE_*` variables. The page doesn't describe isolation beyond the directory, branch, and ports, such as system packages, runtime versions, or OS-level dependencies. Those would need to be handled in your setup commands or outside Paseo.

Paseo has no devcontainer integration. Neither its docs nor my search mention devcontainers, containers or Nix. It also doesn't isolate system packages, runtime versions or OS dependencies per agent. A worktree only gets its own directory, branch and ports.

Consistency comes from two layers, and on Kubernetes they fit together well:

1. **The pod image is the environment.**
   - Agents run as processes inside the daemon container, so what you bake into the child image is every agent's toolchain. That is effectively your devcontainer.
   - You'd bake in `kubectl`, `flux`, `sops`, `talhelper`, `just`, Claude Code and so on, plus the repo's other tools.
   - This also replaces the init container that installs Claude Code now.
2. **`paseo.json` per repo handles per-worktree setup.**
   - `worktree.setup` runs after each worktree is created, for things like `npm ci` or `mise install`.
   - `.worktreeinclude` copies gitignored files such as `.env`.
   - Scripts and services can be defined with ports allocated per worktree.
   - Paseo reads this file from the committed base branch.

Your repo already has a `mise.lock`, so the lowest-effort way to get consistent tools is to put `mise` in the image and run `mise install` in `worktree.setup`. The lockfile then pins versions, and one definition serves both the agents and you. The alternatives are Nix or devbox, which are heavier, or a real devcontainer, which would mean running a container inside the pod. I wouldn't do that.

A few things to know:
- **Secrets and kubeconfig:** Giving agents `age.key` or cluster credentials is a bigger decision than tooling. Anything in `/workspace` or `/home/paseo` is available to every agent. I'd give them a scoped kubeconfig (a ServiceAccount with limited RBAC), not your admin one.
- **Where the repo lives:** `/workspace` is on the PVC, so clone it there once and let Paseo make worktrees from that checkout.

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Build an in-cluster kubeconfig from the pod's mounted ServiceAccount token.
# kubectl has no native "just use in-cluster config" mode (that's a client-go
# thing), so this is the standard workaround.
SA_DIR=/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount
if [ -f "$SA_DIR/token" ] && [ ! -f "$HOME/.kube/config" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$HOME/.kube"
  kubectl config set-cluster in-cluster \
    --server="https://kubernetes.default.svc" \
    --certificate-authority="$SA_DIR/ca.crt" >/dev/null
  kubectl config set-credentials sa --token="placeholder" >/dev/null
  # Point at the token file directly (not the value above) so kubectl picks up
  # kubelet's automatic token rotation instead of using a stale copy.
  sed -i "s#token: placeholder#tokenFile: $SA_DIR/token#" "$HOME/.kube/config"
  kubectl config set-context in-cluster --cluster=in-cluster --user=sa --namespace=default >/dev/null
  kubectl config use-context in-cluster >/dev/null
fi

# gh-app-auth is baked into the image at a fixed path (not under $HOME, since
# the home PVC mount masks whatever the image put there). Symlink it into
# gh's extension dir on $HOME each start — cheap and idempotent.
GH_APP_AUTH_DIR="$HOME/.local/share/gh/extensions/gh-app-auth"
if [ ! -e "$GH_APP_AUTH_DIR" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$GH_APP_AUTH_DIR")"
  ln -s /usr/local/libexec/gh-extensions/gh-app-auth "$GH_APP_AUTH_DIR"
fi

# gh-app-auth's auto-mode git credential helper reads GH_APP_ID and
# GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH from the environment on every git operation (it
# doesn't persist config from `setup`), and it refuses a key file with
# group/other read bits. The secret volume mount is read-only 0644, so copy
# it to a writable, 0600 path each start before wiring the credential
# helper up — cheap and idempotent.
GH_APP_KEY_SRC=/home/node/.github-app/private-key.pem
if [ -f "$GH_APP_KEY_SRC" ] && [ -n "${GH_APP_ID:-}" ] && [ -n "${GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH:-}" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH")"
  install -m 600 "$GH_APP_KEY_SRC" "$GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH"
  gh app-auth gitconfig --sync --auto >/dev/null

  # `claude`, so `git log` doesn't misrepresent autonomous commits as
  # authored by a human. Format is GitHub's standard noreply address for
  # bot accounts: {user-id}+{login}@users.noreply.github.com.

#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail

# Same in-cluster wiring as docker/claude-code/entrypoint.sh (kubeconfig from the
# pod's ServiceAccount token, gh-app-auth git credentials), but $HOME-relative
# since Paseo's home is /home/paseo, then hands off to Paseo's own entrypoint.
# Expects to run as the non-root `paseo` user (the Deployment sets runAsUser 1000).

SA_DIR=/var/run/secrets/kubernetes.io/serviceaccount
if [ -f "$SA_DIR/token" ] && [ ! -f "$HOME/.kube/config" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$HOME/.kube"
  kubectl config set-cluster in-cluster \
    --server="https://kubernetes.default.svc" \
    --certificate-authority="$SA_DIR/ca.crt" >/dev/null
  kubectl config set-credentials sa --token="placeholder" >/dev/null
  # tokenFile (not the value) so kubectl follows kubelet's token rotation.
  sed -i "s#token: placeholder#tokenFile: $SA_DIR/token#" "$HOME/.kube/config"
  kubectl config set-context in-cluster --cluster=in-cluster --user=sa --namespace=default >/dev/null
  kubectl config use-context in-cluster >/dev/null
fi

# gh-app-auth lives outside $HOME in the image (the home PVC masks $HOME).
GH_APP_AUTH_DIR="$HOME/.local/share/gh/extensions/gh-app-auth"
if [ ! -e "$GH_APP_AUTH_DIR" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$GH_APP_AUTH_DIR")"
  ln -s /usr/local/libexec/gh-extensions/gh-app-auth "$GH_APP_AUTH_DIR"
fi

# gh-app-auth refuses a key with group/other read bits and the secret mount is
# read-only 0644, so copy it to a 0600 path each start.
GH_APP_KEY_SRC="$HOME/.github-app/private-key.pem"
if [ -f "$GH_APP_KEY_SRC" ] && [ -n "${GH_APP_ID:-}" ] && [ -n "${GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH:-}" ]; then
  mkdir -p "$(dirname "$GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH")"
  install -m 600 "$GH_APP_KEY_SRC" "$GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH"
  gh app-auth gitconfig --sync --auto >/dev/null

  # Attribute commits to the bot, not whoever is logged into `claude`.
  git config --global user.name "${GH_APP_BOT_NAME:-atmophytes[bot]}"
  git config --global user.email "${GH_APP_BOT_EMAIL:-331837616+atmophytes[bot]@users.noreply.github.com}"
fi

exec /usr/local/bin/paseo-docker-entrypoint "$@"

---
# Paseo daemon (replaces the old `claude rc` devbox). Agents are processes
# inside this one pod: create/destroy them from the Paseo CLI or mobile app,
# no cluster interaction. Reached only over envoy-internal (LAN / WireGuard);
# relay is left disabled (daemon.relay.enabled=false) so nothing goes via
# Paseo's servers. Auth is PASEO_PASSWORD (secret-paseo.sops.yaml).
#
# Name/namespace/SA/PVC/secrets are still `claude-code` on purpose: the home
# PVC already holds the Claude login and the repo checkout, and the
# secret-access Role binds to this ServiceAccount. Rename later if wanted.
#
# Image: docker/paseo (Paseo + the old devbox tooling). devbox-init.sh builds
# ~/.kube/config from the ServiceAccount token and wires gh-app-auth, exactly
# as the old entrypoint did — read-only RBAC in rbac.yaml still applies.
#
# First-time setup, via `kubectl exec -it -n claude-code deploy/paseo -- bash`:
#   claude auth login        # skip if the PVC already has a login
#   git clone https://github.com/bmwinstead/sailing.git ~/sailing
# then add ~/sailing as a project in Paseo. talosctl is already configured
# read-only (os:reader) via the mounted claude-code-talosconfig secret.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: paseo
  labels:
    app: paseo
spec:
  replicas: 1
  strategy:
    type: Recreate # RWO PVC can't be held by two pods during rollout
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: paseo
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: paseo
    spec:
      serviceAccountName: claude-code
      automountServiceAccountToken: true
      securityContext:
        runAsUser: 1000 # `paseo` user in the image
        runAsGroup: 1000
        runAsNonRoot: true
        fsGroup: 1000
      containers:
        - name: paseo
          image: ghcr.io/bmwinstead/paseo:latest
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 6767
          env:
            - name: HOME
              value: /home/paseo
            - name: PASEO_PASSWORD
              valueFrom:
                secretKeyRef:
                  name: paseo
                  key: PASEO_PASSWORD
            - name: PASEO_HOSTNAMES
              value: paseo.${SECRET_DOMAIN}
            - name: GH_APP_ID
              value: "5015762"
            - name: GH_APP_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH
              value: /home/paseo/.local/share/gh-app-auth/private-key.pem
          startupProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /api/health
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
            failureThreshold: 60
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /api/health
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 30
            timeoutSeconds: 5
          volumeMounts:
            - name: home
              mountPath: /home/paseo
            - name: talosconfig
              mountPath: /home/paseo/.talos
              readOnly: true
            - name: github-app
              mountPath: /home/paseo/.github-app
              readOnly: true
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: "250m"
              memory: "512Mi"
            limits:
              cpu: "2"
              memory: "6Gi"
      volumes:
        - name: home
          persistentVolumeClaim:
            claimName: claude-code-home
        - name: talosconfig
          secret:
            secretName: claude-code-talosconfig
        - name: github-app
          secret:
            secretName: claude-code-github-app
            optional: true
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: paseo
spec:
  selector:
    app: paseo
  ports:
    - name: http
      port: 6767
      targetPort: http
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: paseo
spec:
  hostnames:
    - paseo.${SECRET_DOMAIN}
  parentRefs:
    - name: envoy-internal
      namespace: network
      sectionName: https
  rules:
    - backendRefs:
        - name: paseo
          port: 6767

Omnigent is a closer competitor to Paseo than the earlier blog posts suggested, but it solves a bigger problem. These notes come from the Omnigent site and two of its docs pages, not hands-on use.

**What it is.** Omnigent is an Apache-2.0 "meta-harness". A runner wraps each agent (Claude Code, Codex, Pi or your own) in a uniform session, and a server adds shared history and policies. It also ships built-in agents, such as a coding orchestrator and a model-debate agent, and policies like spend caps and model routing. The CLI, web UI, native apps (macOS, iOS and Android) and REST API all talk to that server.

| | Paseo | Omnigent |
|---|---|---|
| Core idea | Chat with and manage coding agents (Claude Code, Codex and others) | A layer above agents: orchestration, policies, sandboxing, shared sessions |
| Mobile | iOS and Android app, connects to your daemon | iOS and Android apps, connect to a server you run (iOS needs HTTPS, which your `envoy-internal` setup already gives) |

# Shared Server Deployment: Summary

**Architecture.** Omnigent has three components:
- **Server:** the central coordinator. It persists session history in a database (Postgres or SQLite), stores artifacts, keeps the catalog of specs, proxies MCP tool calls with policy enforcement, serves skills, and handles auth.
- **Runner:** the per-session process that executes agent loops and harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Claude SDK, etc.). It streams events to the server over WebSocket. The server starts runners on a **host**, which is a machine you register with the server.
- **UI:** the web, terminal, and mobile interfaces. They talk only to the server, never directly to the runner.

**Server deployment options**

- **Docker Compose:** the stack includes the server and Postgres.
  ```
  cd deploy/docker
  ./bootstrap.sh          # generates DB password + cookie secret into .env
  docker compose up -d    # Omnigent server + Postgres
  ```
  On first boot, the server reports `needs_setup`. Create the admin account in the web UI, or preset it with `OMNIGENT_ACCOUNTS_INIT_ADMIN_PASSWORD` for headless deploys.
- **Cloud platforms:**
  - Railway: managed Postgres. You must set the omnigent service's `DATABASE_URL` to `${{Postgres.DATABASE_URL}}`, or the deploy fails.
  - Render: managed Postgres, via one-click deploy.
  - Fly.io: SQLite on a volume, deployed with `fly deploy` from `deploy/fly/`. Use at least 1 GB memory. The server idles around 275 MB.
  - Hugging Face Spaces: SQLite with ephemeral disk. The page says this is for demos only.
- **Databricks:**
  - Managed (recommended, Beta): Databricks operates the server. Enable the Omnigent preview in workspace settings.
  - Self-managed: deploy to Databricks Apps with Asset Bundles, backed by Lakebase (Postgres) and Unity Catalog Volumes, using `deploy/databricks/`. The page recommends this only if the managed service is unavailable in your region or you need custom YAML policies, bring-your-own provider keys, or custom egress controls.
- **Kubernetes:** kustomize manifests in `deploy/kubernetes/`. The `overlays/sandbox-runners` overlay enables the `kubernetes` sandbox provider, which spawns a runner Pod per managed session.
  ```
  kubectl apply -k deploy/kubernetes/overlays/sandbox-runners
  ```

**Key environment variables (Docker)**

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | Postgres connection string |
| `OMNIGENT_AUTH_ENABLED` | Enables multi-user auth (default `1` in Docker) |
| `OMNIGENT_OIDC_COOKIE_SECRET` | Session cookie secret |
| `OMNIGENT_OIDC_ISSUER` | OIDC issuer URL (enables SSO) |
| `OMNIGENT_OIDC_CLIENT_ID` | OIDC client ID |
| `OMNIGENT_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET` | OIDC client secret (omit for public PKCE clients) |
| `OMNIGENT_BUILTIN_AGENT_DIRS` | Extra built-in agent specs or bundles, colon-separated, inside the container |
| `OMNIGENT_SEEDED_AGENTS` | Allowlist of packaged built-in agents shown in the picker |
| `OMNIGENT_FEATURES` | Comma-separated release feature flags; `-name` disables a feature |
| `OMNIGENT_WEB_BASE_PATH` | Serves the server and UI under a path prefix |
| `OMNIGENT_ACCOUNTS_BASE_URL` | Full public URL with prefix, for built-in accounts behind a subpath |
| `OMNIGENT_OIDC_REDIRECT_URI` | Full public callback URL with prefix, for OIDC behind a subpath |
| `OMNIGENT_ENABLE_CANVAS` | Enables Canvas on a self-managed Databricks app (off by default) |

**Other server notes**

- Trimming `OMNIGENT_SEEDED_AGENTS` hides agents from the picker but doesn't delete them. It is not access control, since agents can still be launched by ID through the API.
- Release features are off by default unless noted. The server publishes its feature set at `GET /v1/info`. Restart every replica after changing the value.
- Subpath serving works with prefix-stripping and non-rewriting proxies. The page's example uses code-server's `/proxy/6767/`.

**Runner hosting**

- By default, the host is your laptop: `omni host <server-url>`, after `omni login <server-url>` if auth is enabled.
- Cloud sandbox hosts provide an always-on runner, cloud tooling access, container isolation, and parallel scaling. Supported platforms are Databricks, Modal, Daytona, and Blaxel.
- Runner feature flags, such as `claude_osc_status`, are read from the host's environment, not the server's.

**Gaps in this page.** The page doesn't mention Helm, S3, a default port (other than the `6767` subpath example), or detailed scaling guidance. It only implies that multiple server replicas exist, since the feature-flag section says to restart every replica.

# Omnigent on Kubernetes: Summary

The page covers the base deployment and several overlays in detail. It does not cover some of what you asked about: Claude Code installation and auth in runner pods, runner PVC and persistence, resource limits for runners, warm pools, runner lifecycle and cleanup, or mobile app compatibility. The page points to `overlays/sandbox-runners/README.md` for the runner details, which I don't have.

## Base deployment

- **Deployment:** one pod running `ghcr.io/omnigent-ai/omnigent-server` on port 8000.
- **Service:** ClusterIP, port 80 → 8000.
- **Ingress (optional):** serves HTTPS using cert-manager. It expects a `ClusterIssuer` named `letsencrypt-prod`, which the page says is not shipped.
- **PVC:** 10 Gi at `/data/artifacts` for the artifact store, minted cookie secret, and admin credentials.
- **ConfigMap and Secret:** environment config and database credentials.
- **Prerequisites:** Kubernetes 1.25+, kubectl with Kustomize, and PostgreSQL (managed or in-cluster). Ingress-nginx and cert-manager are needed only for public HTTPS.

Apply the base with:

```
kubectl kustomize deploy/kubernetes/base/ | kubectl apply -f -
```

## Overlays

- **`overlays/postgres/`:** single-replica Postgres 16 StatefulSet with its own 10 Gi PVC. The page says this suits dev and test clusters.
- **`overlays/openshell/`:** provisions NVIDIA OpenShell sandboxes. It needs `OMNIGENT_SANDBOX_SERVER_URL` set and includes RBAC for `AgentSandbox` resources. The included NetworkPolicy allows all egress on 443, which the page says to tighten.
- **`overlays/openshift/`:** replaces the Ingress with an OpenShift Route using edge TLS, plus a `restricted-v2`-compatible SecurityContext.
- **`overlays/openshift-postgres/`:** combines the Postgres StatefulSet, Route, and restricted security contexts.
- **`overlays/sandbox-runners/`:** enables the `kubernetes` managed sandbox provider. A `host_type: managed` session starts one runner Pod that runs `omnigent host` and dials back over the launch-token tunnel. Details from the page:
  - Uses a dedicated runner namespace (`omnigent-sandboxes`, per the ArgoCD section).
  - The server ServiceAccount is least-privilege, with Pod and Secret rights and no `pods/exec`.
  - Uses the official `omnigent-server-kubernetes` image, which adds the `kubernetes` client extra.
  - Model keys such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` come from the `omnigent-creds` Secret, which is projected into every runner Pod.
- **`overlays/argocd/`:** adds `Prune=false` on stateful resources and `ignoreDifferences` for operator-managed Secrets. You must fork the repo because ArgoCD reads from Git.
- **UBI image (`deploy/docker/Dockerfile.ubi`):** uses `ubi9/python-312` and `ubi9/nodejs-20`, and runs as non-root UID 1001.

## Auth

- **`accounts` (default):** username and password. The first visitor claims the instance through the Setup screen.
- **OIDC (optional):** set `OMNIGENT_AUTH_PROVIDER=oidc` and the `OMNIGENT_OIDC_*` variables in a Secret.
- **Accounts caveat:** the page says the built-in `accounts` mode refuses the per-session runner dial-back with a `403`. It calls this a framework-level limit shared by all sandbox providers. Use header/OIDC auth or single-user mode for managed hosts.
- **Header auth:** the page mentions it but does not describe configuration.

## Other notes

- **Feature flags:** set `OMNIGENT_FEATURES` in `base/configmap.yaml`, then run `kubectl rollout restart deployment/omnigent`. Runner overrides such as `-claude_osc_status` must be applied to separately running hosts.
- **Verification:** `kubectl port-forward -n omnigent svc/omnigent 8000:80`, then `curl localhost:8000/health`.
- **Resources:** the server idles around 275 MB RSS. Requests are 512 Mi and the limit is 1 Gi. The first boot against remote Postgres takes about a minute for migrations, so raise the liveness `initialDelaySeconds` to about 90s if the pod is killed on first deploy.
- **Scaling limit:** only one replica is supported because the runner registry is in memory. Don't raise `replicas` without a shared registry such as Redis.

Omnigent does deploy on Kubernetes, but it needs more machinery than Paseo. It also depends on an API key for Claude in runner pods, as far as I can tell.

**What you'd deploy**

| Piece | Details |
|---|---|
| Server | One pod, image `ghcr.io/omnigent-ai/omnigent-server`, port 8000. A ClusterIP Service on port 80. It idles around 275 MB. |
| Database | PostgreSQL is required. An overlay gives a single-replica Postgres 16 StatefulSet with a 10Gi PVC, which the docs call suitable for dev and test. |
| Storage | A 10Gi PVC at `/data/artifacts`. |
| Ingress | Optional, written for cert-manager. You'd use an `envoy-internal` HTTPRoute instead. |
| Packaging | Kustomize manifests in `deploy/kubernetes/`, with no Helm chart. That fits your Flux setup. |
| Runners | The `sandbox-runners` overlay spawns one pod per managed session, in a separate `omnigent-sandboxes` namespace. The server's ServiceAccount can create pods and secrets there, with no `pods/exec`. |

**The good for your goal**
- **Real isolation.** A pod per session is a stronger sandbox than Paseo's one-pod design, and each agent can have its own resource limits.
- **SSO.** It supports OIDC, and your cluster already runs pocket-id. Header-auth mode also works behind a proxy such as oauth2-proxy or Cloudflare Access.
- **Mobile.** The iOS and Android apps connect to a server you run. iOS requires HTTPS, which your `envoy-internal` route already provides. The docs don't mention VPNs, but your WireGuard setup should work, since the only requirement is that the server be reachable from the phone's network.
- **Maturity.** The repo has about 11k stars, 6,000+ commits, and an Apache-2.0 license.

**Concerns**
- **Claude auth.** The docs say model keys such as `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` come from an `omnigent-creds` Secret that is projected into every runner pod. If that is the only path, runner pods use API billing, not your Claude Pro login. I didn't read the `sandbox-runners` README, which should cover this, so I'm not certain. A long-lived registered host that you log in once might work, but that is a guess.
- **One replica only.** The runner registry lives in memory, so the server can't scale out.
- **Docs are drifting.** The Kubernetes README says the built-in `accounts` auth rejects managed-runner dial-backs with a 403. An open issue from yesterday (#12989) says that has been wrong since 0.4.0 and the combination worked on 0.20.0. Nobody on the maintainer side has replied. The same issue says the official image lacks the extras for S3 artifacts or KMS and Vault credential encryption, and that the error only appears at runtime.
- **More moving parts.** It needs Postgres, the server, a runner namespace, RBAC, OIDC wiring and a feature-flags ConfigMap. Paseo is one pod and one password. The repo also shows about 900 open issues.

**Overall:** Omnigent is the stronger choice if you want per-agent pod isolation or policy controls such as spend caps. For a single-user setup that already works, Paseo has far less to maintain. I'd stay on Paseo and look at Omnigent again if you hit isolation or governance needs, or if the subscription-auth question turns out to be fine.

**Claude auth.** The subscription path exists, and issue health is much better than the raw count suggested.

**Claude auth in runner pods**
- **API key:** The `omnigent-creds` Secret takes `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, and it's projected into every runner pod.
- **Subscription:** The sandbox-runners README says to run `claude setup-token` on your own machine and inject the token as `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`. That bills against your Claude plan.
- **Why this works here:** Earlier I found that Remote Control rejects `setup-token` tokens because they can only make model requests. Omnigent runs the agent itself, so model requests are all it needs.
- **Scope:** The Secret is deployment-wide. Every runner pod in the namespace gets the same credentials, and there are no per-user credentials. For a single user that's fine.
- **Git:** Git HTTPS auth comes from a `GIT_TOKEN` in the same Secret. Your cluster uses a GitHub App with short-lived tokens, so that would need an adapter or a PAT.
- **Not documented:** How the Claude CLI gets into the official runner image. The README just says to use "the official multi-arch host image", so I'd verify it runs `claude` before relying on it.

**Persistence is different from Paseo's**
- **Runner pods** are "ephemeral by design". `$HOME` is an `emptyDir` that dies with the pod, and an init container can `git clone` your repo each time.
- **Per-session PVCs** exist only with the `agent_sandbox` provider, as `home-<sandbox-id>` claims.
- **Lifecycle:** The `kubernetes` provider caps a session's Job at 7 days. `agent_sandbox` reclaims an idle sandbox after about an hour and suspends it, keeping the PVC.
- **Session history** lives in the server's Postgres, so conversations should survive restarts, but uncommitted work in a pod's `$HOME` wouldn't.
- **Paseo** keeps everything on one PVC, including repos, worktrees and logins.

**Issue health**
I measured it from GitHub's search API for the last 7 days, as of Nov 6:

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| Opened / closed (7d) | 191 / 244, so the backlog is shrinking |
| Opened / closed (30d) | 893 / 620 |
| Open issues updated in the last 7 days | 310 of 912 |
| Open issues with no activity for 90+ days | 0 |
| Open issues with zero comments | 0 |
| PRs merged (7d) | 429 |
| Releases | Weekly (v0.17.0 through v0.21.0, Oct 6 to Nov 5) |
| Commits | Several today |

That's high churn and not abandonment. A few caveats:
- **Automation:** Every open issue has at least one comment, and #12989 was triaged by a bot. A lot of that activity is probably automated, so it doesn't prove humans respond quickly.
- **Open PRs:** There are 1,378 open PRs, which is a big review queue.
- **Release pace:** Weekly minor versions in the 0.x series means breaking changes are likely.
- **The docs issue:** #12989 is 1 day old with a fix PR (#12991) open, so the doc lag is probably just recent.

**Updated verdict.** Omnigent now looks viable on your cluster.
- **Auth:** The Pro subscription works via `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN`.
- **SSO:** OIDC through your existing pocket-id.
- **Sessions:** A pod per session, with real isolation.
- **Project:** Actively maintained.

The costs are Postgres, a runner namespace and RBAC, ephemeral workspaces by default, and a fast-moving 0.x project. It's still more to run than Paseo, which already does what you asked.

If you want to try it, the cheapest test is a throwaway namespace with the `postgres` and `sandbox-runners` overlays and a `setup-token` credential, run next to Paseo. Should I set that up?
